clue.text: Golden platter backer, as seen by Abou?

parts.note: a platter is slang for a gramophone record, and a golden one is a hit recording
an angel is a financial backer, especially of a stage show

explanation.surface: A financier behind a gold-selling disc, viewed through the eyes of someone called Abou.
explanation.walkthrough: Abou Ben Adhem, in Leigh Hunt's poem, wakes to find an angel writing in a book of gold the names of those who love the Lord; that writer is the recording angel.
explanation.definitionFit: The question mark flags a definition by example: the heavenly scribe in Leigh Hunt's poem is the figure who keeps the record of deeds.

clue.text: The actors aren't polished evidently, but this is rudimentary.

parts.note: something not polished is rough
the actors in a play make up its cast

explanation.surface: A complaint that the performers are unrefined, so the production is basic.
explanation.definitionFit: Roughcast describes something only crudely formed or sketched out, not yet refined, so it is a synonym for rudimentary.

clue.text: Some body is a bounder in the way you'll swear!

parts.note: a bounder is an old word for a cad, a dishonourable man
to aver is to declare solemnly, to swear that something is so

explanation.surface: Someone insists, with an oath, that a particular person is an ill-bred rogue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some body' reads as 'somebody', a person, but it means a body: a corpse.
explanation.definitionFit: A cadaver is a dead body, especially one used for dissection, so it is one particular kind of body.

clue.text: Takes another hitch.

parts.note: a hitch is American slang for a term of military service, so taking another one means signing up again

explanation.walkthrough: A hitch looks like a knot or a lift by thumb; here it is a stint in the armed forces.
explanation.definitionFit: Signing on for a further period of service in the forces is to enlist once more.

clue.text: Disguised CIA post of this, by the very nature of the case.

definitions.text: by the very nature of the case

indicators.note: something disguised has its appearance changed, so the letters of these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A spy's posting is camouflaged by its very nature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disguised' rearranges CIA POST OF; 'this' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means by that very fact, that is, as a necessary consequence of the situation itself.

clue.text: Old circus performers.

parts.note: the circus here is the ancient Roman arena, where armed fighters entertained the crowd

explanation.walkthrough: The circus suggests clowns and acrobats under a big top, but the Roman circus was a venue for combat.
explanation.definitionFit: Roman swordsmen fought for public entertainment in the circus and amphitheatre, so they were the performers of ancient spectacle.

clue.text: The horse sounds so negative, we hear.

definitions.note: read as a verb phrase: what the horse sounds, its call

indicators.note: we hear means the letters entered are a word that sounds like the one the clue gives

parts.note: nay is an old word for no, so negative

explanation.surface: A horse's call seems to be saying no.
explanation.definitionFit: The cry a horse makes is its whinny, the characteristic noise horses utter.

clue.text: Some pipes might be pushed out of the way.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: pipes can have elbows, angled joints, so they are bent at an angle
second meaning: shoved aside with the arm

explanation.walkthrough: The first half needs the answer to finish its sentence: some pipes might be fitted with angled bends.
explanation.definitionFit: Elbow is both a bent pipe fitting and the verb for jostling someone aside with the arm.

clue.text: Drawn by eye, if you're a certain kind of expert.

definitions.text: Drawn by eye, if you're a certain kind of expert.

parts.words: Drawn by eye, if you're a certain kind of expert.
parts.note: a marksman takes aim by sighting along a gun's foresight, an idiom that uses the verb draw

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests an artist sketching freehand; the expert is a sharpshooter, who draws a bead on a target.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw a bead is the idiom for taking careful aim, the bead being the small foresight on a gun barrel.

clue.text: Laundress, but not the French take-off of it…

indicators.note: but not means the following piece is removed from the word before it

parts.note: la is French for the (feminine)

explanation.surface: A washerwoman who is not, apparently, French removes her clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'But not' removes LA, French for 'the', from LAUNDRESS; 'of it' is a link word leading on to the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To undress is to take off one's clothes, so the noun means a stripping off of garments.

clue.text: …and your French friend can make it easy to get along with.

parts.note: ami is French for friend
to be able is to be capable, so it means can

explanation.surface: Continuing the last clue: a French companion can make life agreeable.
explanation.definitionFit: An amiable person is friendly and good-natured, so pleasant company and easy to deal with.

clue.text: Would the English consider them dirty digs?

definitions.text: Would the English consider them dirty digs?

parts.words: Would the English consider them dirty digs?
parts.note: in British English digs are lodgings, so dirty digs are squalid dwellings

explanation.walkthrough: For an American a dig is a jibe or an excavation; the clue points to the British sense, digs as rented rooms.
explanation.definitionFit: A hovel is a small, wretched, dirty house, so filthy lodgings are an apt description.

clue.text: Highly compressed paper saver carried to extremes.

parts.note: something packed hard together is tight
a wad is a compressed bundle of paper, especially banknotes

explanation.surface: A device that squeezes paper hard to save space, pushed to its limits.
explanation.definitionFit: A tightwad is a miser, someone whose saving has gone so far it becomes stinginess.

clue.text: Walker comes across with it, possibly.

definitions.text: Walker comes across with it, possibly.

parts.words: Walker comes across with it, possibly.
parts.note: a person on foot crosses a river or road by means of a narrow bridge meant only for walkers

explanation.walkthrough: 'Comes across with' sounds like handing something over; here it is literal, crossing over by means of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridge for pedestrians only is the structure a walker uses to get across a gap.

clue.text: Thus our exits are made quickly, if you do.

definitions.text: Thus our exits are made quickly, if you do.

parts.words: Thus our exits are made quickly, if you do.
parts.note: leaving a place in a hurry is described by a phrasal verb of rapid departure

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a fire-drill notice; the answer is the phrase for leaving hastily.
explanation.definitionFit: To leave a building at speed is to dash out in haste, a phrasal verb of hurried departure.

clue.text: Steer down here in good time for the winner.

definitions.text: Steer down here in good time for the winner.

parts.words: Steer down here in good time for the winner.
parts.note: steer wrestling is a timed event at this show, where the fastest cowboy to throw a young bull wins

explanation.walkthrough: 'Steer down here' looks like a direction to drive; the steer is a young bullock being wrestled to the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: A rodeo is a cowboy contest whose events, including steer wrestling, are won on the quickest time.

clue.text: Certainly not the right hip in Moscow!

parts.note: red is the colour of the political left, the opposite of the right
the clue's 'certainly not' carries over: the opposite of hip is square, old-fashioned

explanation.surface: A dancer's wrong hip, or an ailing joint, in the Soviet capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Certainly not' governs both halves: not the right gives the left-wing colour, and not hip gives the slang for unfashionable.
explanation.definitionFit: Moscow's great public plaza beside the Kremlin is the place the definition locates in that city.

clue.text: Poetaster — the sort that might be musical.

definitions.note: plural answer: works that might be musical stage pieces

indicators.note: sort is taken as the verb, so the letters of the word are sorted into a new order

explanation.surface: A bad poet whose kind of verse might do as song lyrics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The sort' looks like a noun meaning 'the kind'; it is a command to sort the letters of POETASTER.
explanation.definitionFit: Operettas are light comic operas, short works with music and spoken dialogue, close kin of the stage musical.

clue.text: X □ represents two functions in New York.

parts.note: the multiplication sign, read as times
a box symbol standing for square, the arithmetic function of multiplying a number by itself

explanation.surface: Two mathematical symbols stand for a pair of operations in a New York setting.
explanation.walkthrough: The two functions are arithmetic ones: the times sign and squaring. The copy of this clue shows the second symbol as a U, which gives nothing; a square symbol is what the answer needs.
explanation.definitionFit: Times Square is the famous Manhattan intersection, so the answer is a place found in New York.

clue.text: Certainly not the most bitter time LSD brings out.

indicators.note: brings out suggests the letters are drawn out and laid down in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: An acid trip brings out a person's least bitter moments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brings out' rearranges TIME LSD; LSD is the hallucinogenic drug, here just three letters of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Mild is the opposite of bitter in taste or temper, so the superlative is the least bitter of all.

clue.text: One in carpentry and bricklaying, for example, makes outbursts.

indicators.note: in means the letter for one goes inside the word for skilled occupations

parts.note: carpentry and bricklaying are examples of skilled manual crafts
the Roman numeral I is one

explanation.surface: A worker in the building crafts throws angry fits.
explanation.definitionFit: A tirade is a long angry speech of denunciation, so these are bursts of furious ranting.

clue.text: Language literally belonging to the coast.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the Bantu language of East Africa
second meaning: the name comes from Arabic sawahil, coasts, so it literally means of the coast

explanation.walkthrough: 'Literally' points at the word's origin: Arab traders named the people of the East African shore from their word for coasts.
explanation.definitionFit: Spoken in Kenya and Tanzania, the tongue takes its name from an Arabic word meaning the coastlands.

clue.text: Short rations may be good for the young.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: fare is food, so half of it is a short ration

definitions.text: may be good for the young
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a reduced ticket price that children travel on

explanation.walkthrough: Fare does double duty: food on the table, and the price of a ticket that children often pay at a reduced rate.
explanation.definitionFit: A reduced ticket for children, and literally half the food, a meagre portion; both senses come from the two meanings of fare.

clue.text: Moves, possibly one foot up, with the grain.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: jumps along on one foot, keeping the other raised
second meaning: the flowers of a climbing plant used with malted grain in brewing beer

explanation.walkthrough: 'With the grain' sounds like woodworking; it means the plant that goes into beer alongside barley.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both the verb for springing about on one leg and the plant cones that flavour beer brewed from grain.

clue.text: See 4
See 17 across
Count in German.

parts.note: the German title for a nobleman of the rank of count

explanation.walkthrough: 'Count' could be the verb, asking for a German number word; it is the noble title.
explanation.definitionFit: The German nobility used this title for the rank equal to an English earl or a continental count.

clue.text: Sort of ripe a short month back, as some ears might be.

indicators.note: sort of signals that the word ripe is changed into a different arrangement
back means the abbreviation for the month is read from end to start

parts.note: DEC is the short form of December

explanation.surface: Ears of corn might be a kind of ripe a month early.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of' rearranges RIPE into PIER, and 'back' turns DEC (December, short) into CED. The ears suggest ears of grain ripening; they are human ears with holes for earrings.
explanation.definitionFit: Ears with holes made for wearing earrings are described this way, the result of a quick jewellery-shop procedure.

clue.text: No Pollyanna could make it saltier!

indicators.note: could make it suggests that the letters of the following word can be made into something else

explanation.surface: An endless optimist could never make anything taste saltier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Could make' rearranges SALTIER; 'it' is a link word. Pollyanna is the relentlessly cheerful heroine of Eleanor Porter's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who faces facts plainly is the opposite of a naive optimist like the novel's heroine.

clue.text: Great tennis stars might win with such instant inspiration!

definitions.text: Great tennis stars might win with such
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a brilliant shot from a racket, taken literally
second meaning: a sudden brilliant idea

explanation.walkthrough: The first half reads the idiom literally, as a shot in tennis struck by a gifted player.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a sudden, brilliant idea, and in a tennis match it could describe a match-winning shot.
